subject: chemistry

moments.title: Cavendish notices a residue
moments.body:
Cavendish passes electric sparks through air to combine its nitrogen and oxygen into nitric oxide. He absorbs the products with alkali. A small bubble — about 1/120th of the original air — refuses to react.

Cavendish notes this in passing and moves on. The residue is unidentified for over a century.
moments.takeaway: An anomalous finding sits unexplained for 109 years. Science accumulates loose threads.

moments.title: Rayleigh and Ramsay isolate argon
moments.who: Lord Rayleigh and William Ramsay, Cambridge and London
moments.body:
Rayleigh notices that nitrogen extracted from air is denser than nitrogen made from chemical compounds, by 0.5 percent. Ramsay suggests there's a heavier contaminant in atmospheric nitrogen.

They remove all nitrogen by passing the gas over hot magnesium, leaving a residue that won't react with anything they throw at it. Spectroscopy reveals an unfamiliar emission spectrum. They call it argon ('the lazy one' in Greek). It makes up about 1 percent of air.

quote.text: The new gas has so far failed to combine with any other substance.

moments.takeaway: A new element is hiding in plain sight, in the air everyone breathes.

moments.title: The noble gas family
moments.body:
Ramsay discovers helium on Earth in 1895 (it had been identified from solar spectrum lines in 1868 but not isolated terrestrially). In 1898 he and Morris Travers liquify air and distil out three more: krypton, neon and xenon.

Mendeleev's periodic table has no place for an entire new family. Mendeleev initially resists. Then he and Ramsay agree: the noble gases form a new group (Group 0, now Group 18). The table is extended.
moments.takeaway: A whole new column of the periodic table appears in five years. Existing organising structures can absorb major surprises.

moments.title: Bartlett breaks the noble gases' inertness
moments.who: Neil Bartlett, University of British Columbia
moments.body:
Bartlett is working with platinum hexafluoride, an extraordinarily strong oxidiser. He notices a sample turns red on contact with air. He realises PtF6 has stripped an electron from oxygen to form O2+ PtF6-.

Looking at ionisation energies: O2's first ionisation is 1175 kJ/mol; xenon's is 1170. Almost the same. He tries XePtF6 — and it works. The first noble gas compound exists.

quote.text: I had to look twice to believe it.
quote.attrib: Neil Bartlett, on the first XePtF6 product

moments.takeaway: Noble gases aren't inert after all. The right oxidiser opens up an entire new chemistry.

now.title: Noble gases today
now.body:
Helium is critical for MRI machine cooling, supersonic wind tunnels, gas chromatography and cryogenics. Argon fills incandescent bulbs and shields TIG welding. Neon glows in advertising signs. Krypton and xenon are used in headlamps, ion thrusters and lasers. Radon is a hazard in some basements (radioactive product of uranium decay).

Xenon and krypton have rich fluoride and oxide chemistry. Argon and helium remain genuinely unreactive in normal conditions — but ArF and HArF have been made at cryogenic temperatures.
now.open_questions: Can the lightest noble gases (helium, neon) ever form stable compounds in normal conditions? Why is helium becoming scarce on Earth (it leaks into space), and how should it be conserved? Recent finds: Boncuk gas field in Tanzania discovered helium reserves in 2022.

reflection: Mendeleev's periodic table did not predict the noble gases — they were not 'missing' from his sequence. He had to adapt. How do scientific theories accommodate genuinely unexpected categories of phenomena, and what does it tell us about predictive power?
